📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On a Sunday morning in April, minutes from the US Capitol and down a stretch of Washington, DC’s Pennsylvania Avenue, a wall of black SUVs lined up alongside yellow police tape. Men in military gear held long guns and guarded the entrance to a mirrored window and door.

This is Christ Church DC, a place of worship that appeared on Capitol Hill a year ago.

That Sunday, high-ranking government officials, including Homeland Security's intelligence chief, America’s top international health diplomat, and the government’s international finance chief, had gathered to hear a sermon. “It gives a whole upcoming meaning to worshipping in the presence of your enemies,” quipped the pastor, referencing the church’s location. “We’ve asked the government to fix us, and we’re more enslaved than ever.”.

Christ Church DC arrived after Pete Hegseth, who regularly attends worship with his family, was confirmed as US secretary of defense.

The church is part of Pastor Doug Wilson’s network, known as the CREC—the Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches—which is headquartered in Moscow, Idaho. Wilson’s long-held goal is to turn America into a theocracy, where all its institutions are molded in accordance with biblical law, executions are made public, non-Christians are barred from holding office, and women submit to their husbands instead of voting.

According to recent reports, WIRED has identified around a dozen government officials who have attended services at Christ Church DC at least once since it opened a year ago. Other officials who have attended include a top-ranking Pentagon adviser, a former senior Marine Corps pilot who now oversees personnel affairs in the Navy, and a federal immigration judge with a history of attracting complaints of volatile outbursts toward colleagues.

Wilson calls DC “Babylon on the Potomac,” a biblical moniker he uses to evoke a corrupt place populated by ungodly people. The church has occupied three different locations since it was established, and Wilson has been raising funds to buy a permanent home for it. “We are here for the long haul,” he wrote in a blog post earlier this year. “We believe that it is our responsibility to begin pursuing opportunities to purchase a building near Capitol Hill.” He has also advised on his podcast to not “go to DC and go native” and “[climb] the greasy pole of ambition.” Rather, he said DC “needs an infusion of God-fearing humans.”.

Wilson, who initially agreed to an interview with WIRED and then abruptly canceled with little explanation, hasn’t shied away in past media engagements from touting his newfound clout in government circles. “This is the first time we’ve had connections with as many people in national government as we do now,” Wilson told the Associated Press in 2025, shortly after he came to DC to speak at the opening of his new church.

Wilson’s rising profile and expansion to DC wouldn’t have been possible without Hegseth, says Peter Bell, a researcher, theologian, and host of the podcast Sons of Patriarchy, which has been investigating Wilson for years. “Hegseth gave them an in.”.

“The secretary is a proud member of a church affiliated with the Congregation of Reformed Evangelical Churches, which was founded by Pastor Doug Wilson,” chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told WIRED in response to a request for comment. “The secretary very much appreciates many of Mr. Wilson’s writings and teachings.”.

Parnell subsequently issued a second statement. “Staff at the Department of War have the liberty to practice their faith and attend any church they choose,” he said, using the administration’s name for the Defense Department. “It is shameful that WIRED is attempting to smear respected personnel for exercising their religious freedoms.”.

In 2022, well before he was nominated to President Donald Trump’s cabinet, Hegseth moved his family to the Nashville, Tennessee, area to attend a CREC church and enroll his children in an affiliated classical Christian school. After he was narrowly confirmed as secretary of defense last year, Hegseth introduced a regular monthly Pentagon prayer service and brought out his pastor from Tennessee, Brooks Potteiger, to lead the inaugural session. In July, Potteiger officially became the pastor of Christ Church DC.

“I believe this is significant,” Potteiger said on a podcast with Wilson and other church elders before his move to DC. “It energizes me … to see these young families, and especially the young Christian men, who are hungry for a soaring biblical view of the lordship of Christ over all things.” (Christ Church DC did not respond to WIRED’s request for an interview with Potteiger.).

As secretary, Hegseth has invoked scripture when talking about the war in Iran, established an office of religious affairs at the Pentagon, and used his position to claim that America is a fundamentally Christian nation. "Our department is, you might say, putting on the full armor of God, because while we wage physical war, we all know the real battle is spiritual," Hegseth said in a speech in late September. "Live your calling. Stand firm. Preach truth. Minister to the flock." He has invited Wilson to speak at Pentagon prayer sessions twice this year. In Wilson’s most recent address to the military, just last week, he told his audience why they are right to want America to become a theocracy and why they are right to want to impose a Christian conservative social order.

Sources indicate that wilson, who describes himself as “paleo-Confederate,” has been a fringe figure for decades and operates within a grab bag of historical Protestant traditions. He’s been seeding his influence through his network of around 160 churches and hundreds of CREC-accredited schools and colleges across the US and internationally, laying the groundwork to take his blueprint for a Christian nationalist society well beyond Idaho. Wilson has made it explicitly clear that he is building toward a upcoming political and social order in America—one that places the church at its center and is ruled by Christian men.

Recent findings suggest that through various affiliated media outlets, Wilson has noted “women need to be pastored, and they need to be pastored by men,” and as recently as 2024 he advocated for the repeal of the 19th Amendment, which gave women the right to vote. This belief system goes back decades: In 1996 he coauthored a booklet describing slavery as a “relationship based upon mutual affection and confidence.” He has said that he doesn’t believe that “a Muslim should be able to hold political office” and called immigration a “deliberately fomented war on the American heritage and unremitting hostility to the culture.”.

In a recent development, wilson’s reach into the US government now extends beyond Hegseth. Christ Church DC’s new worshipers include Justin Overbaugh, deputy undersecretary of war for intelligence and security at the Defense department; Nate Halverson, chief of staff to the assistant secretary of the Navy for manpower and reserve affairs; C. Scott “Sonny” Duncan, senior counselor to the secretary of the Navy; Stuart Scheller, senior adviser to the US undersecretary of war for personnel and readiness; and Ryan Higgins, senior adviser for religious complications at the Pentagon and one of Hegseth’s key aides.

Overbaugh, a former US Army officer who was working in risk management in Florida until Hegseth nominated him, now deals with highly sensitive military intelligence and counterintelligence. Overbaugh is an attendee of Christ Church DC and is slated to give a seminar in Tampa, Florida, in January titled “Serving Christ in the Pentagon.”.

Halverson graduated from Latest Saint Andrews College, a university in Moscow, Idaho, that Wilson cofounded, in 2006. In October, despite having no military background, Halverson was appointed chief of staff to the assistant secretary of the Navy for manpower and reserve affairs, another senior Pentagon leadership role that is involved with recruiting all Navy and Marine Corps personnel and oversees policies that impact all military and civilian personnel and their families within the Navy. Prior to joining the Pentagon, Halverson spent 15 years working in sales for Verint, a workforce management software organization.

It has been revealed that duncan, who describes himself as “executive servant leader” on his LinkedIn, was recently promoted to senior counselor to the secretary of the Navy, an influential position that allows him to help shape decisions that impact the entirety of US Navy operations. Duncan is a former Marine pilot who retired in 2023 to fly commercial American Airlines planes and work part-time at Chick-fil-A. His decision to retire with the rank of lieutenant colonel was borne out of his objection to the military’s Covid-19 vaccine requirements, which in turn garnered him positive attention in right-wing media circles.

Last year, Hegseth made Duncan a key point of contact for an initiative titled “Reinstating Service Members Negatively Impacted by the Coronavirus Disease 2019 Vaccination Mandate.”.

Scheller, a former Marine who reached the rank of lieutenant colonel, was court-martialed in 2021 after pleading guilty to showing contempt and disrespect for senior military officials over the chaotic withdrawal from Afghanistan. Higgins, who has also attended the church, was revealed in a recent CNN investigation to have shared scores of racist and homophobic social media posts targeting immigrants and Muslims. Higgins has also played a key role in shaping Hegseth’s Christian nationalist messaging at the Pentagon, CNN reported.

In a recent development, according to data from 2019, 70 percent of active-duty service members identified as Christian. Mikey Weinstein, a former Air Force officer, attorney, and founder of the Military Religious Freedom Foundation, estimates that around half of those adhere to Christian nationalist ideology. For many of those, he thinks that it’s a case of emulating the ideology that they are seeing from their leaders. Weinstein states that the vast majority of the service members that his organization represents are Christians who feel alarmed by and powerless to push back against Christian nationalism that’s taken hold at all ranks, including at the very top.

Government officials outside of the Pentagon are also involved with Christ Church DC.

Recent findings suggest that trump administration couple Bethany and Matthew Kozma have attended the church with their children. Bethany Kozma, the director of global affairs at the Department of Health and Human Services—America's top international health diplomat—is known for her positions against abortion and transgender rights. Matthew Kozma is the Department of Homeland Security's undersecretary for intelligence and analysis and oversees all concerns related to “counterterrorism, counterproliferation of weapons of mass destruction, and critical infrastructure protection.” Both Bethany and Matthew were contributors to Project 2025.

Industry observers note that the church has also attracted some personnel from the Justice Department, including David Vandenberg, who was hired to the DOJ’s civil rights division last year and was seated last month as an immigration judge. He worked in Fresh Mexico and Texas as an assistant US attorney from 2021 to 2024. In Texas, Vandenberg’s colleagues complained of alleged volatile behavior.

Recent findings suggest that brantley Mayers, a former fellow at the Claremont Institute, a right-wing think tank, works as counsel to the assistant attorney general for the DOJ’s civil division. Mayers was often a spokesperson for the DOJ, defending the Trump administration’s ICE occupation of Minneapolis earlier this year. He was also referred for discipline in June after a federal judge ruled that the DOJ had engaged in “unsettling” practices in its efforts to get a Rhode Island hospital to comply with a subpoena over transgender care. “That is dirty pool, in my opinion, and the Department of Justice have willfully done that in this case,” the judge said at a May 2026 hearing. Mayers represented the DOJ at a hearing for this case.

Recent findings suggest that another church attendee is Stephen Duggan, chief financial officer at the US International Development Finance Corporation, which invests in private-sector development projects overseas. (Earlier this year, the head of the DFC was questioned by Congressional Democrats about the agency’s investments and their “potential entanglements” with the Trump family.) In the past, Duggan worked as the chief financial officer for Bentkey Ventures, a subscription-based streaming service that offers “anti-woke” children’s content and is owned by the media manufacturer The Daily Wire.

It has been revealed that andrew Braun, defense policy adviser for Mike Rounds, a GOP senator from South Dakota and former government relations manager at the conservative think tank The Heritage Foundation, has also attended church services. Paul Lindstrom, who was briefly an offensive lineman for the University of Idaho Vandals football team and worked as an executive assistant in the Office of the President until recently, has attended, as has Samuel Brown, undersecretary for memorial affairs at the Department of Veterans Affairs.

(WIRED reached out to all the government officials mentioned in this story for comment. None of them replied with the exception of a spokesperson for Bethany Kozma, who initially denied that she’d ever attended the church. When told that WIRED was entirely confident that Kozma had attended at least once, the spokesperson said she would call back and never did.).

At the church, these officials rub shoulders with members of conservative think tanks, delegates from the CREC network, judicial clerks, venture capitalists, lobbyists, and more.

Recent findings suggest that having like-minded Christians in office is a core part of Wilson’s long-term strategy. “Wilson is explicit concerning his desire to see Christians in office—and only Christians in office—and a church at the foot of the Capitol is the clearest route toward that end,” says Bell.

Recent findings suggest that A core part of Project 2025, the blueprint for Trump’s second term in office, was a plan to infuse Christian nationalist ideology into all levels of US government. Shortly after taking office, Trump signed an executive order that established a task force to investigate “anti-Christian bias” in government departments, and Christian nationalists were placed in key roles. Across the government, and beyond the Pentagon, this attitude has been replicated: The former secretary of labor began a monthly prayer service months after the creation of a White House Faith Office.

“Doug, in his own words, has always specified a Christian culture comes from the ground up rather than being imposed, and that is crucial here,” said Bell. “Put Christians in office, legislate Christian morality, let that simmer among the populace, and Christian culture eventually emerges.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, the species, known as Aptostichus stephencolberti, is a trapdoor spider that lives in California's coastal dunes.
  • In a recent development, many spiders reach their largest size in the fall after spending the summer feeding, making them familiar symbols of Halloween.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A tiny California spider named after comedian Stephen Colbert is making a big impression on scientists. Although it is only about the size of a quarter, the spider has a genome roughly 50% larger than the human genome.

According to recent reports, the species, known as Aptostichus stephencolberti, is a trapdoor spider that lives in California's coastal dunes. Its unusually large genome seems particularly fitting given Colbert's famously pompous television persona on the former Comedy Central show "The Colbert Report.".

In a recent development, many spiders reach their largest size in the fall after spending the summer feeding, making them familiar symbols of Halloween. But this particular spider stands out for something that cannot be seen with the naked eye: the extraordinary amount of DNA packed into its tiny body.

"At 4.6 gigabases, or 4.6 billion DNA base pairs, it's not the largest genome among the spiders, but it's significant," stated corresponding author Jason Bond, a professor in the UC Davis Department of Entomology and Nematology.

According to Bond, this is the first time scientists have sequenced the genome of a spider belonging to this family. The findings were published in the Journal of Heredity.

A Secretive Spider That Hunts From Underground.

Visitors to the coastal dunes of Northern California may unknowingly pass close to these spiders without ever spotting one. Most of their lives unfold beneath the sand, where they remain hidden in carefully constructed burrows.

In a recent development, female trapdoor spiders spend their entire lives underground in tunnels lined with silk. Each burrow has a hinged entrance that blends into its surroundings, allowing the spider to stay concealed while monitoring activity outside.

When an unsuspecting insect or other prey animal approaches, vibrations alert the spider to its presence. At precisely the right moment, the spider bursts through its hidden door to capture its next meal.

Although these spiders are skilled ambush predators, their venom poses no danger to humans. Bond noted that among the more than 50,000 known spider species, only about 30 to 50 have venom known to be toxic to people.

A Spider Genome Bigger Than the Human Genome.

Industry observers note that the spider's DNA contains more surprises than its sheer size. Researchers found that its genome includes 52 chromosomes, compared with the 46 chromosomes typically found in human cells, which are organized into 23 pairs.

However, having a larger genome does not necessarily mean having more genes. In this spider, approximately 77% of the genome consists of repetitive DNA sequences that appear many times throughout its genetic material.

The research also highlights an unusual feature of spider chromosomes. Spiders lack the conventional repetitive DNA sequences associated with telomeres, the protective structures at the ends of chromosomes. This difference could help explain why spider chromosomes appear to evolve more rapidly than those of vertebrates.

"It lends itself to broadening our understanding of spider genome composition and consequently how genomes have evolved across the animal Tree of Life," Bond stated.

Why Is the Spider Named After Stephen Colbert?

The story behind the spider's unusual scientific name dates back to 2008, when Stephen Colbert discovered that Bond had named a trapdoor spider after rock musician Neil Young.

It has been revealed that not wanting to be left out, Colbert turned the situation into a comedy segment. During "Who's Not Honoring Me Now?" on "The Colbert Report," he publicly demanded that Bond name a spider in his honor.

Bond agreed, and Aptostichus stephencolberti became Colbert's namesake in the spider world.

Rising Seas Threaten California's Trapdoor Spiders.

Beyond revealing the spider's genetic peculiarities, the research could play an important role in protecting the species.

The genome sequencing effort is part of the California Conservation Genomics project, a state-funded initiative designed to build a collection of genomic information that scientists can use to guide conservation decisions.

Trapdoor spiders generally do not venture far from their burrows, making it difficult for populations to move between habitats. Because their coastal dune environments are already separated into isolated areas, researchers hope genetic information will help them identify distinct populations that may need special protection.

In a recent development, "We Californians love our beaches and trapdoor spiders share them with us," Bond mentioned. "We're hoping to understand how things like climate change, fire and urbanization might be impacting the genetic diversity of species.".

Aptostichus stephencolberti (the "t" in Colbert is silent) is found only in coastal dunes along a limited stretch of Central California, extending from the San Francisco Bay area to Monterey.

Recent findings suggest that this restricted range makes the species particularly vulnerable to environmental changes. Rising sea levels could eliminate portions of its coastal habitat, while invasive species pose another significant danger.

"They're going to be incredibly sensitive to sea-level rise, but they're also very sensitive to invasive species," Bond said.

Spider Venom Could Hold Clues to Latest Medicines.

Recent findings suggest that the potential benefits of studying this spider's genome extend beyond conservation and evolutionary biology. Scientists also hope that understanding spider genetics will help them explore the vast range of chemical compounds found in spider venom.

Some substances identified in spider venoms have shown promise as potential painkillers, while others could be useful in developing new ways to control agricultural pests.

With so many spider species still poorly understood at the genetic level, researchers believe their venoms may contain valuable compounds that have yet to be discovered.

"We don't really know what's out there in terms of untapped natural product diversity for venoms," Bond noted.

Sources indicate that the study's additional authors include Stephen Richards, Emma Jochim, Lacie Newton, James Starrett, Ruta Sahasrabudhe and Oanh Nguyen of UC Davis; Eric Beraut, Colin Fairbairn, Samuel Sacco, William Seligmann and Merly Escalona of UC Santa Cruz; Robert D. Cooper of Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University; and H. Bradley Shaffer and Erin Toffelmier of UCLA.

The research received support from the California Conservation Genomics Project, with funding provided to the University of California through the state of California's State Budget Act of 2019, as well as from the National Science Foundation.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Police in several locations across Germany reported large numbers of bomb threats targeting schools.

They stated that while they were investigating the claims, they did not initially have reason to treat them as credible threats.

More than 400 schools in the southwestern state of Baden Württemberg received threats, and more than 250 in Saxony-Anhalt received the emails, with several other regions also targeted on Monday morning.

Police in Erfurt in Thuringia were among the first to issue a statement on the threats, saying they were responding to threats at "multiple schools" after morning warnings, including in Jena, Erfurt, Mühlhausen, Zella-Mehlis, Nordhausen, Gotha, Rudolstadt and Greiz.

"The same word-for-word threats were received this morning at the various eductional institutes," police wrote in a press release. "Based on preliminary findings other federal states are also affected by the threatening messages.".

Police stated they had no information yet on the potential author or sender of the emails. They were investigating breach of the peace-based crimes via the threat of criminal activity.

"At present the police is not working on the assumption of the bomb threats being serious and recommends that schools do not implement evacuation measures and continue their normal operations," they said.

Police in Freiburg in the southwest and authorities to the north in Hanover also said they were responding to emailed bomb threats directed against schools.

Similar reports are emerging to the north of Germany in Denmark.

As in Germany, Danish police remarked they did not believe the threats were credible, "but they understandably create insecurity locally at the schools.".

This follows other recent cases of coordinated bomb threats against multiple schools that turned out to be hoaxes in Italy earlier in the month.

It also comes amid various apparent bids to create disruption within Europe in recent weeks, such as multiple bomb threats targeting commercial airlines, or hacking into supermarket refrigeration systems to spoil produce en masse.

#150531. A Former DOGE Operative Won a Federal Contract. Then Things Got Messy

A Former DOGE Operative Won a Federal Contract. Then Things Got Messy

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yet another former member of the so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) appears to have exited the government only to return as a contractor.
  • In September, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) put out a call for a contract worth $200,000 for “modernization discovery, prototyping, and implementation-planning engagement.” Four days later, the department closed the bidding process and awarded the contract to Yat Choi LLC, a organization owned by a former Airbnb engineer and Canadian citizen named Yat Choi, whose company also goes by the name GovMaxxing.
  • According to recent reports, at the time, Choi had left his role at the National Design Studio (NDS)—the group tasked with redesigning government websites—just a few weeks prior.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yet another former member of the so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) appears to have exited the government only to return as a contractor.

In September, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) put out a call for a contract worth $200,000 for “modernization discovery, prototyping, and implementation-planning engagement.” Four days later, the department closed the bidding process and awarded the contract to Yat Choi LLC, a organization owned by a former Airbnb engineer and Canadian citizen named Yat Choi, whose company also goes by the name GovMaxxing.

According to recent reports, at the time, Choi had left his role at the National Design Studio (NDS)—the group tasked with redesigning government websites—just a few weeks prior. Before that, Choi worked at DOGE.

In a recent development, the bid was for a project set to run for a little under six months, and the contract was awarded as sole-source, meaning that it did not go through a normal competitive bidding process. In the documentation announcing the award, HHS justified this decision by saying that its “market research and source rationale found that conventional consulting firms generally would need to assemble a multidisciplinary team or obtain additional technical resources” to provide the required skills around “business-process modernization, artificial intelligence, automation, technical architecture, and rapid prototyping.”.

In October, a company called CoA Solutions lodged what’s known as a bid protest with the Government Accountability Office (GAO) contesting the agency’s decision to award the contract to Choi. CoA Solutions is a small business that builds AI software for the government and received another contract with the Treasury Department in 2024.

Ari Perez, the CEO of CoA Solutions, tells WIRED that his company made a bid below the $200,000 award price, and it proposed two experts doing the work full-time, including Perez himself.

Sources indicate that perez claims that CoA asked HHS for an explanation of the award on October 8 and, when it did not receive one, filed its protest with the GAO the next day. Perez says that his company’s sole contestation was about how the bids were evaluated by HHS, not about Choi or his work with NDS.

“I'm a service-disabled veteran. I've served this government since I was 17 at West Point. At the US Digital Service I helped deliver for veterans at the VA, and later I worked on asylum and immigration systems at DHS. I started CoA to keep doing impactful government work,” says Perez. “We want to win on merit, and if HHS reopens it, we'll bid again.”.

According to recent reports, according to CoA, in response to the bid protest, HHS terminated the award to Choi and canceled the call for contractors. With the cancellation, the GAO dismissed the protest without investigating it further. A GAO spokesperson referred WIRED to HHS.

“HHS remains committed to modernizing its systems to improve efficiency and better serve the American people,” notes HHS spokesperson Grace Davis Jamison. “Following a bid protest challenging the award, HHS voluntarily took corrective action, terminating the contract at no cost to the government and canceling the solicitation.”.

In a recent development, choi’s role in the US government has not been exactly clear. In his bio on X, Choi writes that he was part of both DOGE and NDS, and noted in a post that he was recruited by billionaire Elon Musk and Joe Gebbia, Airbnb’s cofounder, to help modernize the retirement system at the Office of Personnel Management (OPM). Gebbia now leads NDS, which was created after Musk left government and which has served as a landing pad for several DOGE members, including Edward “Significant Balls” Coristine.

In December 2025, Choi contributed to a blog on the NDS website about automating the federal retirement system. But on his LinkedIn, Choi lists himself as a senior technologist at OPM. On November 5, just two days after Republicans lost the midterm elections, Choi announced in a post on X that he had left OPM and was launching his company, GovMaxxing, through which he aims to continue to contract with the government. GovMaxxing operates as Yat Choi LLC federally.

In response to questions from WIRED about his role in government, Choi notes that he “was recruited to support federal modernization efforts and subsequently onboarded as an OPM contractor.” There, Choi says, he “contributed to modernization efforts associated with DOGE and subsequently NDS. I was not, and have never been, a federal government employee.” Choi claims he left OPM in mid-August, though OPM did not respond to questions confirming whether this was the case. “I began actively pursuing the contracting opportunity after my engagement with OPM ended,” says Choi.

Choi confirmed that he is a Canadian citizen and a “lawful permanent resident” of the US. Foreigners are not generally allowed to hold full-time roles in government or serve as special government employees. The rules are more flexible for contractors. During the height of DOGE’s activity, a close Musk ally, Baris Akis, was prevented from joining the group as a special government employee because he is a Turkish citizen, according to The Atlantic. Akis, however, continued to serve as a recruiter for the group.

On his website, Choi labels the “client” for his work in government as “US Office of Personnel Management / DOGE / National Design Studio” and describes himself as the “modernization lead.” However, documents indicate that Choi’s company was not registered in the state of Upcoming York until April 2026, and in the System for Award Management, the procurement website where US government contractors bid, there are no other contracts for Choi’s work. “None of my work at OPM was performed through my LLC. My website references my prior professional experience at OPM and does not attribute that work to my company,” claims Choi.

Choi claims that the HHS contract was for a “separate modernization discovery project. It was not a continuation of any work with OPM, DOGE, or NDS.”.

Sources indicate that according to the code of federal regulations, except in very specific circumstances, government contracts cannot be awarded to government employees or to organizations they fully or partially own. But Jessica Tillipman, associate dean for government procurement law studies at George Washington University, claims that even though Choi was not a regular government employee, the fact that he was part of DOGE and NDS, whose work has spanned across government agencies, could create the appearance of a conflict of interest with regard to the HHS contract. “The baseline posture of the federal acquisition regulation is to strictly avoid conflicts of interest or even the appearance of them,” says Tillipman. “So agencies all have a duty, and the contracting teams have a duty, to make sure that they are considering these things when they're awarding these contracts.”.

Choi tells WIRED that HHS “initiated contact and expressed interest” in his “modernization experience” before the call for bids was revealed. HHS did not respond to questions about whether the bid had been written specifically for him.

Tillipman notes that while the government may sometimes create a contracting opportunity designed for a specific person or manufacturer, “it’s generally niche or highly specialized work." Tillipman says that the fact that there were 75 bids placed on the contract indicates that this is “not a unique service.” She notes that the government’s justification for a sole-source contract is “thin.” “Usually, when there's only one responsible source, there's a technical reason,” she says. This could be something like a special tool that is not interoperable with outside software, or when there is only one company that can provide a specific service or that makes a certain physical part that might be used for weapons or specialized machinery.

In a recent development, on the GovMaxxing website, Choi notes that potential government clients can work with the company as a prime contractor or “subcontract through one of our partner primes your agency may already be working with.” Unlike prime contracts, there is no way to publicly see which subcontractor a prime contractor works with. Choi declined to name the companies or current “prime” contractors he subcontracts under.

It has been revealed that but Tillipman indicates that even if Choi were to take on another version of the HHS contract for a subcontractor, similar questions could still be raised within the agency and externally should it ever come to light. “In certain instances, your subcontractors’ conflicts can be imputed to the prime contractor,” she says. “The whole thing is highly irregular overall.”.

Choi is not the only former DOGE or NDS member who appears to be hoping to benefit from federal contracts after leaving the government. Earlier this year, WIRED reported that Ethan Shaotran, one of the young engineers who formed the early core of DOGE, had started a defense tech startup. The startup has been listed on the System for Award Management since April. Former DOGE members Jack Stein, Gavin Kliger, Luke Farritor, and Marko Elez introduced an AI defense technology manufacturer called Cathedral, which has been listed on the System for Award Management since July. Neither have received “prime” contracts with any federal agency, but whether they have been taken on as subcontractors to other prime contractors is unclear.

In a recent development, despite the HHS contract’s cancellation, Choi appears undeterred. Earlier this week, following the nationwide grounding of flights by the Federal Aviation Administration, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called for funding to modernize air traffic control in a post on X. In response, Choi wrote, “Secretary Duffy, I’m the DOGE engineer who led the modernization of federal retirement processing at OPM last year … I’ve since started a firm to work with more agencies, and we’d love to help with the FAA’s modernization efforts. Put us in, coach!”.

Industry observers note that apple's most affordable and most vibrant laptop has only been out since this past March, but it sounds like the company will offer a spiffy upcoming upgrade sooner rather than later. That's hardly a surprise, given the success of the product so far.

Sources indicate that that's what Mark Gurman of Bloomberg is reporting, anyway. That timing is meant to line up with the iOS/macOS 27.4 upgrade cycle, at which point Gurman indicates we could also see the iPhone 18 and 18e models, a fresh OLED iPad Air, and a new budget iPad.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

Sources indicate that as for what to expect from the fresh MacBook Neo, it doesn't sound like a hugely substantial upgrade at this point in time. From a usability standpoint, the most important thing Gurman mentioned is that the A18 Pro chip powering the original Neo will be upgraded to an A19 chip, with RAM bumped from 8GB to 12GB as well.

It has been revealed that it remains to be seen if the current $699 starting price for the MacBook Neo will go up, but it's definitely a possibility. We do live in a RAMageddon world, after all, and Apple has already raised the price of the Neo once. It's also worth pointing out that the A19 chip powering the Neo 2 would still be less capable than the M-series chips powering more expensive Mac computers. Even the upcoming iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max have an A20 Pro chip.

Sources indicate that beyond the chip improvement, Apple is also looking to add new MacBook Neo colors "frequently," per Gurman. However, Gurman didn't say for certain whether or not that will start with the second iteration of the budget laptop. The first version came in silver, indigo, blush, and citrus, so Apple definitely has room to add even more hues for people to enjoy.

#150527. Tech Report: Rejecting cheap fabrics, higher prices: Why shoppers are asking for better clothes

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1292 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Rejecting cheap fabrics, higher prices: Why shoppers are asking for better clothes

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1292 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Clothing isn't made like it used to be, and more shoppers are taking notice.
  • Sources indicate that the makeup of apparel imported into the U.S.
  • According to recent reports, apparel prices generally declined over the two decades leading up to the pandemic, according to the consumer price index.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clothing isn't made like it used to be, and more shoppers are taking notice.

Sources indicate that the makeup of apparel imported into the U.S. has shifted in recent years. In 2010, about 60% of clothing was predominantly made from cotton. Now, that total is around 45%, while predominantly synthetic fabrics such as polyester and nylon comprise the majority of imports.

According to recent reports, apparel prices generally declined over the two decades leading up to the pandemic, according to the consumer price index. Since 2020, they have soared to record highs.

Industry observers note that it's starting to change habits for consumers who are paying more for food, gas, rent and other staples. As shoppers shell out more for clothes, they're increasingly making sure the garments are worth the cost.

Consulting firm AlixPartners' 2026 Consumer Sentiment Index, which surveyed more than 9,000 shoppers, found that consumers are scrutinizing labels more closely and rejecting cheap materials sold at a premium.

"If it's not a natural material, a retailer brand who passes it off as it is, they're really becoming very low on consumers' minds," noted Sonia Lapinsky, head of fashion at AlixPartners.

Fast fashion brands like Forever 21 and H&M exploded in popularity during the early 2000s and 2010s, bringing trendy clothing to shelves promptly at low prices. Then came ultra-fast fashion, with brands like Shein and Fashion Nova pumping out newly introduced garments at even quicker speeds and lower price points — made possible in part through the use of inexpensive, synthetic fabrics.

"We got to a point where the pendulum just swung too far in that direction. And we've actually begun to see a reversal," mentioned U.S. Bancorp BTIG consumer analyst Janine Stichter. "Quality matters a lot more ... over the last three or four years than it has in the previous 10 or 20.".

But quality, which shoppers often tie directly to material, can come at a higher cost.

It has been revealed that the average unit price of apparel imported to the U.S. between January and August was $2.64 per square meter for garments that were predominantly synthetic fiber, like polyester and nylon, compared with $3.67 for items that were largely cotton, according to data from the U.S. Commerce Department's Office of Textiles and Apparel.

When comparing those 2026 figures to 2010, synthetic fiber apparel import costs have climbed around 11%, while cotton apparel costs have risen 21%.

"If you're appealing to a more value-sensitive customer, you either reduce the quality, or you negotiate with suppliers to try to share some of the cost or you maybe absorb the cost … and perhaps hope to crank a higher volume of product to make up for it," mentioned Bernstein Research senior retail analyst Aneesha Sherman.

Recent findings suggest that though polyester is cheaper, experts point out that's not necessarily a bad thing. It can help clothing hold its shape and wick away sweat.

In a recent development, sherman believes the athleisure boom is a primary factor in the shift toward polyester. She said that from 2015 to 2025, sports apparel was growing at a 4.9% rate in the U.S., versus 2.6% for all apparel and footwear, according to Euromonitor data.

Recent findings suggest that "There probably is some quality trade down as well happening there," Sherman noted. "But I think both these trends are conflated.".

Nonetheless, backlash to synthetic materials is growing. Gen Z has even repurposed the word "polyester" as an insult to mean generally low-quality or fake.

Concerns have also grown about the environment and human health surrounding petroleum-based clothing, as more research indicates microplastics can leach from polyester clothing when washed.

It's led consumers to reexamine what materials are in their clothing.

Recent findings suggest that apparel prices have risen coming out of the pandemic, as demand outpaced supply and allowed companies to raise prices, stated BTIG's Stichter. Tariffs and the Iran war followed, raising costs for businesses — and prices for consumers.

Petroleum is the basis of many synthetic fibers, and oil prices have skyrocketed since the start of the Iran war.

The same factors that helped drive up prices of clothing — Covid, tariffs and war — also affected clothing quality.

"Companies had to move around their supply chains in the post-Covid period," stated Stichter. "They had to find ways to take costs out, and sometimes that meant using less expensive fabrics.".

Those factors compounded a more-than-decade-long shift away from manufacturing in China.

Sheng Lu, a fashion and apparel studies professor at the University of Delaware, whose research focuses on the economics of the global textile industry, said China's established history with clothing production means it has higher-skilled workers, state-of-the-art-equipment and better material management compared with emerging manufacturing destinations such as Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Cambodia.

According to recent reports, "They mostly serve the value market and the mass market. And I think the reason why they're not ready to make higher-quality luxury and premium products really reflects the kind of skill sets you can expect when you source from these countries," said Lu.

Recent findings suggest that alixPartners' Lapinsky said these countries that manufacture at a lower cost sometimes have to still ship the raw materials from China, which can extend the timeline to make clothing. That means taking earlier bets on trends and then discounting if products don't sell well.

"If you have to mark down that product because the consumer doesn't want it as much, your net margin might actually be worse than if you were to just invest in quality in the first place," said BTIG's Stichter.

And as material costs rise for synthetic fibers, Stichter also stated she believes it could further influence companies to use more natural fabrics moving forward.

Companies prioritizing quality are winning in this environment.

Ralph Lauren's stock is up around 85% over the past two years. Around 90% of its apparel is primarily made of cotton, leather, wool, viscose, cashmere or silk, according to its 2026 sustainability report. In its fiscal 2026, the company noted it sold more products at full price and reduced markdowns.

Meanwhile, direct-to-consumer clothing brand Quince, which centers its brand identity around natural materials, reached a $10 billion valuation this year.

Sources indicate that the brand jumped 16 spots to No. 3 for best resale value in online consignment retailer ThredUp's 2025 report. Organic cotton retailer Pact jumped 20 spots on that list to No. 8, illustrating the potential role materials are playing in brand recognition.

Alternatively, the 2026 AlixPartners report, which ranks sentiment for brands in different retail categories, found shoppers are viewing some fast fashion brands less favorably. Both Shein and Zara dropped three spots — to fifth and seventh place, respectively — in terms of sentiment in the young adult specialty category.

Shein passed higher tariff costs onto shoppers in 2025 and then blamed a sales slowdown on those higher prices. The ultra-fast fashion retailer saw its year-over-year share of U.S. apparel, accessories and footwear card spending decrease in the fourth quarter of 2025 and first two quarters of 2026, according to Consumer Edge.

Shein did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Though Zara fell in AlixPartners' Consumer Sentiment Index, it has continued to grow sales and profits year over year. Even so, Lapinsky noted worsening consumer views are something to watch, even if the company is doing well.

"What we found over the years with this consumer sentiment index is that sometimes it will be a bit of a leading indicator of what's to come," said AlixPartners' Lapinsky. "I'm not saying that this is going to be true for Zara, but I think that's one thing that we'll be watching as we look in the upcoming quarters and into 2027.".

Finland's Prime Minister Sanna Marin concedes election

📅 02 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 2 min read (489 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Finland’s left-wing Prime Minister Sanna Marin conceded defeat on Sunday in the Nordic country’s parliamentary election as the opposition right-wing National Coalition Party (NCP) claimed victory in a tightly fought contest.
  • The pro-business NCP was expected to win 48 of the 200 seats in parliament, narrowly ahead of the nationalist Finns Party with 46 seats and Marin’s Social Democrats on 43 seats, justice ministry election data showed with all ballots counted.
  • “We got the biggest mandate,” NCP leader Petteri Orpo said in a speech to followers, vowing to “fix Finland” and its economy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finland’s left-wing Prime Minister Sanna Marin conceded defeat on Sunday in the Nordic country’s parliamentary election as the opposition right-wing National Coalition Party (NCP) claimed victory in a tightly fought contest.

The pro-business NCP was expected to win 48 of the 200 seats in parliament, narrowly ahead of the nationalist Finns Party with 46 seats and Marin’s Social Democrats on 43 seats, justice ministry election data showed with all ballots counted.

“We got the biggest mandate,” NCP leader Petteri Orpo said in a speech to followers, vowing to “fix Finland” and its economy.

He will get the first chance at forming a coalition to obtain majority in parliament as Marin’s era as prime minister was expected to end.

Popular abroad, at home Marin faces battle to keep her job.

“We have gained support, we have gained more seats (in parliament). That’s an excellent achievement, even if we did not finish first today,” the prime minister remarked in a speech to party members.

Marin, 37, the world’s youngest prime minister when she took office in 2019, is considered by fans around the globe as a millennial role model for progressive new leaders, but at home she has faced criticism for her partying and her government’s public spending.

Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin takes drug test following partying backlash.

While she remains very popular among many Finns, particularly young moderates, she antagonized some conservatives with lavish spending on pensions and education they see as not frugal enough.

The NCP has led in polls for almost two years although its lead had melted away in recent months. It has promised to curb spending and stop the rise of public debt, which has reached just over 70% of GDP since Marin took office in 2019.

Orpo accused Marin of eroding Finland’s economic resilience at a time when Europe’s energy crisis, driven by Russia’s war in Ukraine, has hit the country hard and the cost of living has increased.

Orpo has said he will negotiate with all groups to obtain a majority in parliament, while Marin has said her Social Democrats may govern with the NCP but will not go into government with the Finns Party.

Marin called the Finns Party “openly racist” during a debate in January – an accusation the nationalist group rejected.

Recent findings suggest that the Finns Party’s main goal is to reduce what leader Riikka Purra has called “harmful” immigration from developing countries outside the European Union. It also calls for austerity policies to curb deficit spending, a stance it shares with the NCP.

Most notable of Marin’s foreign policy actions has been her push, along with President Sauli Niinisto, for the country to make a watershed policy U-turn by seeking NATO membership in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

That process is now almost complete, with Helsinki expected to join within days after all the Western defense alliance’s 30 members approved the accession.

RIIZE brought their online fandom into the real world. I was there to see it.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1840 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, that was one of my first thoughts on Friday night as I watched K-pop group RIIZE perform for roughly 600 fans at Brooklyn Steel in New York City.
  • Recent findings suggest that it's a funny contradiction, considering the entire premise of the evening was to bring digital fandom into the physical world.
  • In a recent development, the occasion was Spotify CLOSER, a new live music series that brings artists and their most dedicated listeners together for intimate performances and conversations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We need to bring back MTV Unplugged.

According to recent reports, that was one of my first thoughts on Friday night as I watched K-pop group RIIZE perform for roughly 600 fans at Brooklyn Steel in New York City. There were no elaborate stage productions or arena-sized crowds. Instead, there were stripped-down performances, candid conversations, a few wonderfully awkward moments, and a sea of smartphones held high above the audience.

Seriously, everyone had their phones out.

Recent findings suggest that it's a funny contradiction, considering the entire premise of the evening was to bring digital fandom into the physical world. But maybe that's just what being a fan looks like in 2026. Even when we're standing a few feet away from our favorite artists, we still want to capture the moment, preserve it, and inevitably share it with everyone who couldn't be there.

In a recent development, the occasion was Spotify CLOSER, a new live music series that brings artists and their most dedicated listeners together for intimate performances and conversations. After launching in Seoul in Oct., the series made its U.S. debut on Nov. 20 with RIIZE, bringing together more than 600 fans from the New York tri-state area, many of whom were identified as the group's top local listeners and selected based on their listening habits.

Since debuting under SM Entertainment in 2023, RIIZE — consisting of Shotaro, Eunseok, Sungchan, Wonbin, Sohee, and Anton — has emerged as one of K-pop's most prominent fifth-generation acts, performing at major festivals like Austin City Limits and Lollapalooza South America. But despite their growing international popularity, the group has only toured the U.S. once, making opportunities for American fans to see them in person relatively rare.

For many, their relationship with RIIZE has largely unfolded online, through music, livestreams, social media, and the seemingly endless stream of content that makes K-pop fandom feel like a full-time commitment.

In other words, the same platform that connected these fans to RIIZE's music was now bringing them face-to-face with the six people behind it. And I was curious to see what would happen when that connection moved offline.

Before RIIZE even took the stage, Spotify had transformed Brooklyn Steel into something of a playground for BRIIZE, the group's devoted fandom.

There was a fisheye photo station, branded Spotify x RIIZE microphone keychains, and an area where fans could write letters to the members. Nearby, six lockers offered a glimpse into each member's personality, decorated with objects representing their individual interests.

Shotaro's locker featured a camera and bucket hat, while Eunseok's included boxing gloves and a Doraemon plushie. Sungchan's was outfitted with a soccer ball and cleats, and Wonbin's displayed Nike Air Force 1s and earbuds. Sohee's locker featured a Boston cap and Naruto figures, while Anton's contained a violin and swimming goggles. Each member had also written a personal letter to BRIIZE.

For longtime fans, these weren't just random objects. They were familiar details, the kinds of things you pick up from watching livestreams and behind-the-scenes content. You can know an idol's favorite foods, recognize their sense of humor, and feel familiar with their friendships without ever having met them. Seeing these details arranged in physical space felt a little like stepping inside the digital world fans had spent years getting to know.

And that was the interesting thing about the event. Spotify wasn't simply bringing fans closer to RIIZE by putting them in a smaller room. It was recreating the familiarity of online fandom in a setting where fans could participate, leaving their own messages alongside the members' handwritten notes.

Of course, once RIIZE appeared, nearly every phone in the room went up, mine included. So much for going offline.

Sources indicate that the crowd was enthusiastic and eager to interact, with handwritten signs scattered throughout the audience. My personal favorite was a sign directed at Anton that simply read, "Slap me." (I have questions, but I respect the commitment.).

Recent findings suggest that anton, who grew up in Fresh Jersey, received particularly enthusiastic cheers from the Garden State contingent. There was also a very crucial geography lesson in which fans informed the members that Peter Parker, aka Spider-Man, is from New York. You know, the essential cultural exchange that happens when a K-pop group visits the city.

These were the kinds of interactions that made the evening feel less like a conventional concert and more like a gathering of people who already knew one another, even if most of them had never actually met.

And for RIIZE, it was an opportunity to put faces to the streaming numbers.

RIIZE opened the night with "Get A Guitar," their 2023 debut single, performed entirely in English for the first time. The setlist also included "Boom Boom Bass," "Impossible," "D-D-Done," "Love 119," and the first U.S. performance of "Do your dance.".

It has been revealed that but the evening wasn't just about the music. Between performances, the members participated in a Q&A hosted by Anton, who served as the group's unofficial emcee and occasional English translator. He kept the conversation moving, prompting his bandmates to answer questions and helping bridge the language gap with the predominantly English-speaking audience, while live subtitles appeared on the screens.

Initially, the members seemed a little reserved. Away from the familiar structure of a performance or the carefully edited chaos of variety content, there was a certain shyness to their early exchanges, as though they were still finding their footing in a more spontaneous setting.

But as the Q&A progressed, that initial hesitation gave way to something more playful. The members began teasing one another, laughing more freely, and engaging with the crowd. Sohee, in particular, seemed to come alive as the night went on. Funny, expressive, and naturally charismatic, he grew increasingly comfortable commanding the room, revealing a different side of the confidence he already brings to the stage as one of the group's standout vocalists.

It was fun to watch that transformation happen in real-time.

Sources indicate that during one segment, the members voted on which of them best fit a series of superlatives. Sungchan was named the funniest, Anton earned the title of biggest flirt, and Shotaro received a unanimous vote for best smile. The conversations were sometimes silly, occasionally awkward, and all the more charming for it.

My favorite exchange came when Shotaro was expressing his appreciation for the fans. After delivering a heartfelt message, he earnestly added, "Please forget that.".

Anton was quick to correct him: "Please don't forget that.".

That small moment captured the easygoing charm of the night. RIIZE are a group accustomed to the precision of rehearsed performances, but here, in front of hundreds of fans, they were navigating something far less predictable. There was no choreography to fall back on, no script for a misplaced word or an unexpected laugh. Just six guys figuring it out together, and letting their personalities shine in the process.

For all the playful banter and fan interactions, the moment that stayed with me most was RIIZE's performance of their latest single, "Insomnia.".

The song is already one of the group's more understated offerings, performed without choreography, but for Spotify CLOSER, RIIZE took that intimacy a step further with a fresh, even more stripped-down arrangement. The performance put the focus squarely on their voices, allowing their harmonies to shine and giving the song a different kind of emotional weight. There was something lovely about hearing a song that was already relatively restrained given even more room to breathe.

It was the closest the evening came to the spirit of MTV Unplugged, the iconic music series that invited artists to reinterpret their work in a more intimate setting.

That's not to say RIIZE needed to abandon the choreography or elaborate performances that are so integral to K-pop. But there's something special about hearing artists approach their own material from a different perspective, especially when it brings out details that might otherwise go unnoticed.

Watching "Insomnia," I found myself missing that kind of music programming — the opportunity to see artists experiment with familiar songs, to hear their voices in a upcoming context, and to experience a performance that feels entirely specific to a particular room and moment.

Spotify CLOSER isn't quite Unplugged, nor does it need to be. But the appeal feels similar. Sometimes, hearing a familiar song in a different way is enough to make you appreciate it all over again.

According to recent reports, there's a certain irony in a streaming platform creating an event designed to bring fans away from their screens. Especially when nearly everyone in the room was holding up a phone.

Spotify CLOSER is, of course, a branded experience. It's a way to reward highly engaged listeners while creating exclusive content that can eventually circulate on the platform. Select performances from the evening will be released on Spotify, allowing fans around the world to experience some of what happened in Brooklyn.

But the commercial nature of the event doesn't make the connection any less meaningful. If anything, the night illustrated how intertwined our digital and physical experiences of fandom have become.

Industry observers note that the fans at Brooklyn Steel didn't leave their online identities at the door. They brought their phones, their handwritten signs, their knowledge of the members' personalities, and all the inside jokes and shared references they'd accumulated from following RIIZE online. And the members, who initially seemed a little timid, gradually relaxed into the kind of playful, slightly clumsy interactions fans have come to love through their screens.

As the evening drew to a close, RIIZE expressed their hopes of returning to Newly introduced York before ending with an encore performance of "One Kiss.".

For all the ways technology has made artists more accessible than ever, there's still something it can't quite replicate: the spontaneity of sharing a room, where a mistranslated word can become a joke, a fan's sign can spark a conversation, and a familiar song can sound entirely upcoming.

And for the record, Shotaro, I won't forget that.

COP deadlock prompts calls for a reset of climate diplomacy

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (983 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The longest-running climate talks in history came to a disappointing conclusion on Sunday as negotiators failed to come to an agreement on a shared political direction on climate change.
  • After two days of extended talks, representatives from country after country, tiredness etched into each face, voiced their opposition to the so-called "Antalya Pact.".
  • "I understand that there is no agreement on this text.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The longest-running climate talks in history came to a disappointing conclusion on Sunday as negotiators failed to come to an agreement on a shared political direction on climate change.

After two days of extended talks, representatives from country after country, tiredness etched into each face, voiced their opposition to the so-called "Antalya Pact.".

"I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted," noted Murat Kurum, Turkish president of the COP31 climate summit.

One of the main sticking points: the words "fossil fuels." While some nations, including petrostates like Saudi Arabia and Russia, wanted them omitted from the text, others saw it as a "step backwards" not to include them.

It has been revealed that around 130 parties — among them vulnerable island nations, developing countries and richer EU members — called for the reintroduction of the two words into the text, to no avail. And so many refused to support the adoption of the final COP agreement.

The deadlock signals a failure for the UN process. But the number of countries willing to walk away from what they saw as a weak text was, arguably, a show of strength, and one that had been long coming.

The phrase "fossil fuels" first appeared three years ago in the closing decision of COP28 in Dubai with the promise of "transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems, in just, orderly and equitable manner." But it has been omitted from every text since.

Yet this year's climate summit was the first to acknowledge that the world will breach the critical 1.5-degree Celsius (2.7-degree Fahrenheit) threshold that scientists noted would safeguard the world from the worst impacts of planetary heating.

In a recent development, and so, the pressure was on for progress; to turn pledges from previous years into concrete action. But that progress didn't come.

"We don't celebrate the deep divisions exposed or the lack of a political signal from COP31 capable of driving climate action in line with science, equity and the law," mentioned Nikki Reisch, director of the climate and energy program at the Center for International Environmental Law.

"But the rejected text would have done more harm than good.".

The lack of agreement was not solely about fossil fuels; money also played a part.

Developing nations have long argued that they need additional financing, both as a means for them to move away from coal, oil and gas, but also to help them cope with the consequences of rising temperatures.

According to recent reports, countries all over the world are being battered by extreme weather events. Catastrophes like flooding, drought and wildfires have been fueled and worsened by rising global temperatures. Often the worst hit are poorer countries with low rates of greenhouse gas emissions.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

And yet, richer states behind much of the historical emissions are increasingly unwilling to foot the bill. Dissatisfaction at home due to higher food and fuel prices has left many governments loathe to pay more to finance climate action abroad.

With the United States  — the world's biggest historical emitter  — now absent from negotiations and on the verge of leaving the United Nation's Framework Convention on Climate Change, the European Union was portrayed as this year's villain with some observers accusing the EU of hypocrisy.

"You can't demand action and then block the finance that makes this possible," Fanny Petitbon, policy analyst at 350.org, noted in a statement.

As the world's largest provider of climate finance, the EU reportedly refused to negotiate on providing additional finance and has repeatedly called for other nations to step up.

The failure to find an agreement is a particularly bitter turn of events for countries that face ever worsening impacts of climate change, like the island states that are being confronted by a reality that could see their countries wiped off the map as sea levels rise.

Although the Turkey-led electrification agenda calling for an increase in global electricity consumption to 35% by 2035 was not formally adopted — it made up part of the rejected final agreement — more than 90 countries pledged to move forward regardless.

Recent findings suggest that it's not a silver bullet. There was no agreement on ensuring the increase was forged only through clean, renewable energy. But it would still signal forward momentum, driven by economic forces and a need for home-grown energy security.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Industry observers note that and there are other hopes. The second conference on the Just Transition Away from Fossil Fuels will take place in Tuvalu in July 2027. Initiated at the COP30 conference last year in Belem, Brazil, it has seen increasing support from countries putting together concrete roadmaps for abandoning coal, oil and gas.

According to recent reports, there has been much talk of blame and who is responsible for the breakdown and collapse of talks. What is clear is that the UN climate summits need reform. Progress, when it does happen, is slow. The present model, based on consensus, requires all countries to agree on every measure. There have been many calls for majority-rule decision making, which might have forced the inclusion of language like "fossil fuels" into the text.

Recent findings suggest that but ultimately, this is not the time to focus on fault. As the climate crisis accelerates, governments need to reflect — and quickly — on what can be done outside of these UN processes, within their nations, to speed up climate action.

"The take-home message from COP31 is clear: the world must do much more to confront the climate crisis — and it must do it now," remarked UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres in a statement.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bola Tinubu (in red hat) would be 79 at the end of a second term, if he is re-elected.

Abdulhadi Dalhatu is something of a rarity in Nigeria politics.

At 38, he is among the young people seeking elected office in a country where about 80% of the population is under 40.

He hopes his age will stand in his favour as he campaigns for a seat in the state assembly in the northern Kano state in January's general elections.

"Younger people are the majority in this country and should be deciding the future," Dalhatu tells the BBC.

But Nigeria's political history suggests he faces an uphill battle.

Since the return to civilian rule in 1999, Goodluck Jonathan has been the youngest person elected president, taking office at the age of 53.

The current president, Bola Tinubu, is 74 and would be 79 by the end of a second term if he is re-elected in January.

His main challengers are also considerably older. Atiku Abubakar, seeking the presidency for the seventh time, is 79, while Peter Obi is 65.

Of the 18 presidential candidates, only one is under 40 - Moses Olusoji Adebisi, a 35-year-old businessman representing the Democratic Leadership Alliance (DLA).

Although he states he is confident of winning, few Nigerians appear to know much about him and he has not been seen much on the campaign trail.

The contrast is striking in a country with one of the world's youngest populations, where young people have repeatedly demonstrated their ability to shape political debate and mobilise for change.

In the previous election, Obi, then 61, galvanised millions of young Nigerians through a social media-driven movement known as the "Obidients".

His campaign promised a break from the established political order, appealing particularly to young people struggling to find jobs and earn a decent living.

But his failure to win the presidency left many of his supporters disillusioned.

"At the time we were so hopeful, but unfortunately the result wasn't what we wanted, which made many lose hope in the system," former Obedient Nonso Chukwudi tells the BBC.

The movement had built on the momentum of the EndSars protests in 2020, which grew into one of Nigeria's biggest youth-led movement in decades.

Initially sparked by anger over police brutality, the demonstrators developed into a wider call for political reform, accountability and greater youth participation in governance.

According to recent reports, but the protests were eventually crushed by the authorities. About 56 were reportedly killed, although officials dispute this figure, while hundreds were arrested and some had their bank accounts frozen.

Both EndSars and the Obedients demonstrated the capacity of young Nigerians to mobilise around political causes.

Abdulhadi Dalhatu hopes to be president one day but bemoans the financial obstacles needed to contest.

But turning that enthusiasm into sustained electoral participation has proved much harder.

It has been revealed that hajara Musa, 33, is among those who have lost faith in the political system. She has no aims to register or vote in the near future.

In a recent development, "I just feel like things are already determined and I'll just be wasting my time. It is going to be the same people all over again," she tells the BBC.

The electoral register appears to reflect this growing disillusionment.

Although the number of registered voters has increased by 10 million to over 103 million since the last election, enrolment of those under 35 has actually fallen, by about seven million.

Young people now account for just 29% of registered voters, down from 40% in 2023.

Nigeria's electoral commission, Inec, claims it has made efforts to encourage more young people to register ahead of the 2027 general elections.

This includes appointing nine ambassadors from the entertainment industry, spanning film, music and comedy, to reach younger audiences.

But the figures suggest these efforts have yet to make a significant difference.

Dalhatu claims he understands the frustration but argues that young Nigerians cannot expect change, if they stay away from the political process.

"Unfortunately, many prefer to just post on social media" instead of getting involved, he notes.

Of course being young does not mean you are necessarily the best candidate.

For those who want to participate, there is a formidable obstacle to getting into politics - money.

Young people now account for just 29% of registered voters, down from 40% in 2023.

Dalhatu dreams of becoming president one day, but says he has previously had to abandon campaigns because he could not raise enough funds.

The cost of running for office in Nigeria is notoriously high.

Under the Electoral Act, presidential candidates were allowed to spend up to 5bn naira (Â£2.8m; $3.7m) on campaigns ahead of the 2023 elections. That spending limit has since been doubled.

The cost of nomination forms alone puts the presidency beyond the reach of most aspiring young Nigerians.

The ruling All Progressive Congress (APC), along with the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and the African Democratic Congress (ADC) have each set their presidential nomination fee at 100m naira ($74,000; Â£56,000), making it extremely hard for latest challengers to emerge.

Since the return to democracy in 1999, only two parties have governed Nigeria - the PDP from 1999 to 2015 and the APC since 2015.

These parties, alongside the ADC, formed last year by politicians who had defected from the other two, have established nationwide network of branches, supporters and campaigners.

Those aspiring candidates without the financial resources to secure nomination forms and compete in the internal party contests of the main parties have little chances of becoming president.

The barriers are also evident in the National Assembly.

Not one of Nigeria's 109 senators is under 40, while only 14 of the 360 members of the House of Representatives fall into that age group.

"I have been in politics for many years and I will tell you that young people in this country lack the resources to become president," states Dalhatu, who is running under Obi's Nigeria Democratic Congress.

Atiku Abubakar is seeking the presidency for a seventh time.

Fatima Zahra Umar, a young politician in the APC who has previously tried to run for a seat in the House of Representatives, agrees.

"Young Nigerians are poor. Nigerian politics is cash-intensive, so participation is guided by money," she indicates, adding that young people are often content with having a bit of influence as a special advisor to a senior politician.

But political analyst Seun Ajayi believes the problems go beyond the financial barriers.

"We have some of the most brilliant young persons in the world, but they are either not interested in politics or feel satisfied when given a small role in government," he says.

"The old men are not going to sit idle and allow us to push them out. We have to fight for the significant positions, but at the moment I don't see the zeal.".

Umar believes changing attitudes towards young leadership is equally notable.

"Culturally, we are not primed to trust or accept the brilliance of a younger person, so it will be very difficult," she claims.

"Old men are still holding on to the system.".

Some Nigerians took inspiration from the wave of success of young candidates in the recent midterm elections in the US, some of whom have roots in Africa.

"America Has Done It, Can Nigerians Do the Same?" entertainer Charly Boy wrote on X, in a post that was widely shared.

He noted the US results served as a warning to Nigerian politicians that no matter how powerful the political machine, voters can change the direction of government.

In a recent development, he called on young people to interrogate candidates about their past promises: "Has life improved? Where are the jobs, security and affordable living?

"Democracy is not a spectator sport, nor is it about sharing rice," he wrote.

💡 Key Takeaways
